newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end off on techs, supply and Lindsey.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end off on techs, supply and Lindsey.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed lower for the third consecutive session on Wednesday, dragged down by technical selling, fresh corporate supply and bearish comments from a top Federal Reserve official, analysts said.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended down 11/32 at 98-30/32. Its yield was at 6.83 percent.
Analysts said the selling bout gained momentum in mid- afternoon trade after Federal Reserve governor Lawrence Lindsey said curbing inflation may mean a temporary rise in future interest rates.

Speaking from prepared remarks, Lindsey said in Dallas that, "while the commitment of the Federal Reserve to preserving a low inflation is unwavering, I cannot assure you that all politicians feel the same way.
"Nor can I guarantee you that sustaining the fight against inflation will not mean a temporary rise in interest rates at some time in the future."
The market took Lindsey's words as a warning. But the fact that the Fed governor has been a little more "hawkish" in his latest remarks tamed the comments a bit, analysts said.

"Lindsey appears to be tilting towards the hawkish side again," said Josh Stiles, senior strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc. "He really sounded that way before the Federal Open Market Committee met (on September 24) as well. That encouraged more long liquidations."
Analysts said a technical selling that started in the futures market and spilled into the cash trading also weighed on prices on Wednesday.
The December futures bond contract broke the 200-day moving average of 110-25/32 late in the session in the Chicago Board of Trade, igniting a technical selling spree.
Large new corporate and asset-backed supply combined with the market's hangover after the Treasury's 10-year note auction on Tuesday also pushed prices down.
"When we tried to rally this morning we were hit with selling related to heavy corporate and asset-backed supply in the market," Stiles said.

Rumors, later denied, concerning the health of Russian leader Boris Yeltsin also made a dent on prices early in the session. Russian and U.S. officials dashed the rumors that Yeltsin's health had deteriorated considerably.
"There was a rumor about Yeltsin when the market began to sell off," said John Spinello, managing director of government securities trading at Merrill Lynch and Co. Inc.
"But when people realized there was no substantiation to the rumor the market stabilized and rallied a little bit. But it still seems like it's under some supply pressure," he said.
Analysts said money managers were mostly on the selling side on Wednesday. But some foreign buying was spotted very early in the session, they added.
"There was some talk of hedge fund buying and some central bank buying. But in the afternoon, we've seen a like amount of selling from some money managers," said a top trader.

On the economic data front, the market continued to brace for the release on Friday of the producer price index (PPI) and retail sales for September. In the meantime, analysts said, consolidation seems to be the word.

"Over the last few days, the market has been solidifying the view that...the Fed is kind of on hold for now and the economy does seem to be slowing," said Josh Feinman, global markets economist at BT Securities.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed down one basis point at 4.99 percent. The six-month bill rate was flat at 5.10 percent. The year bill rate was unchanged at 5.25 percent.

The two-year note closed down 1/32 at 100-3/32, yielding 5.95 percent. The five-year note traded off 3/32 at 100-9/32 to yield 6.31 percent. The 10-year note closed down 3/32 at 99-20/32, yielding 6.55 percent.
